paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from 1998, its leaf grown in Menghai County in Yunnan. On a label, [Menghai](menghai-county:county-and-factory) can mean the county or the tea factory of the same name, which blends leaf from several mountains. Here it names the county where the leaf grew.

The leaf was fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making) but never dried with hot air afterwards. That leaves some of the leaf’s own activity alive, and that activity is what lets the tea keep changing in the cake for years.

At twenty-eight years it is past both points where the trade says [aged](sheng:ageing) raw pu’er begins: ten years for some, twenty or more for many. Raw pu’er is not given shou’s rapid fermentation, so this cake has changed slowly in [storage](sheng:aging). How it was kept is as much a part of its history as its age.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
